subtopics.title: Natural resources and their classification
subtopics.theory_md:
A **natural resource** is anything from the environment that humans use: air, water, soil, forests, minerals, fuels, sunlight.

By renewability:
- **Inexhaustible**: not used up by use (solar, wind, tidal).
- **Renewable**: regenerate naturally within a human time scale (forests, fresh water, soil, fish).
- **Non-renewable**: fixed stock formed over geological time (coal, petroleum, natural gas, uranium, minerals). Consumption $\gg$ formation. Metals can be recycled; fossil fuels cannot.

By origin: **biotic** (forests, animals, fossil fuels) and **abiotic** (water, air, minerals).

Years a non-renewable stock lasts: $R/P = \text{proven reserves}/\text{annual production}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a bank account. A renewable resource is a salary that arrives every month. A non-renewable one is a lump sum: every withdrawal leaves less, and nothing is paid back.
key_points: Natural resource defined with examples
Three classes: inexhaustible, renewable, non-renewable, with two examples each
Non-renewable: consumption far exceeds formation (finite stock)
Coal, petroleum, gas, uranium and minerals are non-renewable; metals are recyclable

subtopics.title: When a renewable resource becomes non-renewable
subtopics.theory_md:
A renewable resource stays renewable only while **use rate $\le$ regeneration rate** (sustainable yield). If use exceeds regeneration for long, the stock collapses and the resource behaves as non-renewable.

- **Forests**: felled or burnt faster than they regrow (short jhum cycle, timber felling); barren land follows.
- **Groundwater**: pumped faster than rain recharges (Punjab, Haryana); the water table keeps falling.
- **Soil**: 2.5 cm of topsoil takes several hundred years to form but erosion can remove it in a few years.
- **Fish and wildlife**: overfishing and hunting cause extinction, which is irreversible.

Conservation: 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), efficiency, substitution by renewables.
subtopics.basics_md: A well refills from rain. Draw a bucket a day and it stays full. Draw ten buckets a day and it runs dry, and then it is as good as a resource that never refills.
key_points: Renewable only if use $\le$ regeneration (sustainable yield)
Overuse exhausts the stock, so it behaves as non-renewable
Examples: forests, groundwater, soil, fish or wildlife
Remedy: 3Rs, efficiency, renewable substitutes

subtopics.title: Uses of forests and their ecological role
subtopics.theory_md:
Forests cover about 21.7% of India (ISFR 2021); the National Forest Policy 1988 target is 33% (two-thirds in hills).

**Commercial uses**: timber, fuelwood, pulp and paper, bamboo, gums, resins, lac, medicinal plants.

**Ecological services**:
- Carbon sink: absorb $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in photosynthesis and release $\mathrm{O_2}$.
- Watershed: regulate the water cycle, recharge groundwater, reduce floods.
- Roots bind soil, preventing erosion and landslides.
- Habitat for most terrestrial biodiversity; local climate control.

**Deforestation and global warming**: removing trees removes the sink, and burning or decay of felled wood releases stored carbon as $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
subtopics.basics_md: A forest is a giant sponge, filter and air-conditioner at once. It soaks up rain, holds the soil with its roots and takes carbon dioxide out of the air.

subtopics.title: Deforestation: causes, effects and remedies
subtopics.theory_md:
**Causes**: agriculture, **shifting cultivation** (jhum, North-East India: cut, burn, farm 2-3 years, abandon; the fallow cycle has shrunk from 20-30 to 2-5 years), **overgrazing** (seedlings eaten and trampled, no regeneration), fuelwood and timber, mining, dams, roads, urbanisation, fires.

**Effects**: loss of biodiversity, soil erosion, **floods** (more runoff), **droughts** (less transpiration and rain), **landslides** (roots no longer bind the soil), siltation of reservoirs, more $\mathrm{CO_2}$, desertification.

**Dams**: submerge forest, fragment habitat, displace tribal people.

**Remedies**: afforestation, social and agro-forestry, Joint Forest Management, planting trees, paperless work, recycling, protected areas.
subtopics.basics_md: Roots are like nails holding a hillside together. Cut the forest and the nails are gone, so rain washes the soil down and the stream floods.
key_points: Causes: shifting cultivation, overgrazing, agriculture, timber, mining, dams
Jhum: short fallow cycle, forest cannot regrow; overgrazing stops regeneration
Effects: biodiversity loss, erosion, flood, drought, landslide, global warming
Remedies: afforestation, social forestry, JFM, recycling

subtopics.title: Water on Earth and why its properties matter
subtopics.theory_md:
Earth's water is about **97.5% saline**; only **2.5% is fresh**, mostly as ice and groundwater, and under 1% is easily usable. India has about 18% of the world's people but about 4% of its fresh water.

**Falkenmark indicator** (per-capita availability): stress below 1700, scarcity below 1000, absolute scarcity below 500 $\mathrm{m^3/person/yr}$.

**Properties that matter**: high **surface tension** (with cohesion and adhesion: capillary rise of water in tree trunks); high specific heat; **universal solvent**; liquid from 0 to 100 °C; **anomalous expansion** (densest at 4 °C, so ice floats and aquatic life survives under it).
subtopics.basics_md: Almost all water is salty, and most of the fresh part is frozen or deep underground. The water we can actually use is a tiny fraction.

Falkenmark: stress < 1700, scarcity < 1000 $\mathrm{m^3/person/yr}$

subtopics.title: Aquifers and overuse of groundwater
subtopics.theory_md:
An **aquifer** is a permeable underground layer (sand, gravel, porous sandstone) that stores groundwater and yields it freely to wells. It may be **unconfined** (open to recharge from above) or **confined** (between impermeable layers).

**Good aquifer**: porous and permeable (sand, gravel). **Clay** is porous but has tiny pores and very low permeability, so it is an aquiclude, a bad aquifer.

**Overuse of groundwater**: falling water table, drying wells, land subsidence, sea-water intrusion in coastal areas, more arsenic and fluoride in deep water.
**Overuse of surface water**: dries rivers downstream, destroys wetlands.
subtopics.basics_md: Water sits in the gaps between grains. Big connected gaps (sand, gravel) let it flow to a well. Clay has gaps too, but so tiny that water barely moves.

subtopics.theory_md:
**Dam benefits**: irrigation, hydropower, drinking water, flood control, fisheries.
**Problems**: displacement of people, submergence of forest, siltation, waterlogging and salinity in the command area, reservoir-induced seismicity, loss of fish migration.

subtopics.title: Floods, droughts and rainwater harvesting
subtopics.theory_md:
**Floods**: heavy rain made worse by deforestation, siltation and encroachment of flood plains. **Droughts**: failed monsoon made worse by over-pumping, deforestation and water-intensive crops. Both are partly man-made.

**Conservation**: rainwater harvesting, watershed management, check dams, drip and sprinkler irrigation, reuse of treated wastewater.

**Rooftop harvesting potential**: $V = A \times R \times C$ with $A$ catchment area ($\mathrm{m^2}$), $R$ annual rainfall (m, convert mm to m), $C$ runoff coefficient. $1\ \mathrm{m^3}=1000$ L.
subtopics.basics_md: Rain falling on a roof is free water. Catch it in a tank or send it underground, instead of letting it run into the drain.
key_points: Floods and droughts have human causes

subtopics.title: Types of mining
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Open pit / surface mining**: overburden removed in layers; shallow deposits (iron ore, coal, limestone). Strips vegetation and clears **vast areas of forest**.
- **Sub-surface (underground) mining**: shafts and tunnels reach deep deposits (coal, gold); leaves **large cavities underground**, causing subsidence.
- **Placer mining**: loose alluvial deposits of heavy minerals (gold, tin, sand) recovered by **dredging** or **hydraulic mining** (high-pressure water jets).
- **In-situ leaching**: ore dissolved in place by a chemical solution (e.g. copper, uranium), little surface disturbance.
- **Auger mining**: boring into a coal seam on a hillside.

subtopics.title: Fertilisers, pesticides and the Green Revolution
subtopics.theory_md:
The **Green Revolution** (HYV seeds, irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides; M.S. Swaminathan) made India grain self-sufficient but brought problems.

**Fertilisers (NPK)**:
- **Nitrate** leaching: nitrate over 45 mg/L in drinking water causes **blue baby syndrome**, as nitrite converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin.
- N and P runoff: **eutrophication**.
- Micronutrient imbalance, soil acidity.

**Pesticides** (DDT, BHC): persistent and fat-soluble, so they **biomagnify** up the food chain; pest resistance; death of beneficial organisms. Remedy: integrated pest management, biopesticides (neem), organic farming.
subtopics.basics_md: Fertiliser dissolves and washes into water; pesticide stays and piles up in fat. So fertilisers cause algal blooms and nitrate poisoning, while DDT builds up in birds at the top of the food chain.

subtopics.title: Waterlogging, salinity and sustainability of agriculture
subtopics.theory_md:
**Waterlogging**: over-irrigation and canal seepage raise the water table into the root zone; roots lack oxygen.

**Salinity**: in arid areas evaporation from the waterlogged soil leaves salts ($\mathrm{NaCl}$, $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$) at the surface (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan). High osmotic pressure stops roots taking up water; sodium destroys soil structure; yield falls and land becomes barren.

**Remedies**: drainage, drip irrigation, flushing, gypsum for sodic soils, salt-tolerant crops.

**Pesticide long-term effects**: persistence, resistance, loss of beneficial organisms, contamination.
subtopics.basics_md: Too much irrigation brings the water table up. When it evaporates, it leaves its salt behind like the white ring in a kettle, and crops cannot grow in it.
key_points: Mechanism: high water table, evaporation, salt left behind
Effects: osmotic stress, poor soil structure, barren land
Remedies: drainage, drip, gypsum, salt-tolerant crops

subtopics.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
subtopics.theory_md:
**Fission**: slow neutron splits $\mathrm{^{235}U}$; chain reaction sustained and controlled by **moderators** (heavy water, graphite) and **control rods** (Cd, B). It is the commercial nuclear power today (Tarapur, Kudankulam).

$\mathrm{^{235}_{92}U + ^{1}_{0}n \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}Ba + ^{92}_{36}Kr + 3\,^{1}_{0}n}$ + about 200 MeV

**Fusion** (D-T): $\mathrm{^{2}_{1}H + ^{3}_{1}H \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}He + ^{1}_{0}n}$ + 17.6 MeV. Needs about $10^8$ K to overcome repulsion; no material holds the plasma; confinement (tokamak, ITER, lasers) has not given sustained net energy, so it is **not yet practical**. It would be cleaner (little long-lived waste, abundant fuel).
subtopics.basics_md: Fission is splitting a heavy nucleus, which happens at ordinary reactor temperatures. Fusion is forcing two light nuclei together, which needs the heat of the sun. We can do the first on a large scale; not yet the second.

subtopics.title: Solar, hydro, tidal and wind energy
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Solar**: photovoltaic cell (doped **silicon** or **gallium** arsenide semiconductor) converts light directly to electricity. Sun is the ultimate energy source of the biosphere (photosynthesis).
- **Hydro**: $P=\eta\rho g Q H$; needs perennial river with large head: **Himalayas** (Tehri, Bhakra).
- **Tidal**: needs coast with high tidal range: Gulf of Khambhat, Kutch, Coromandel coast; not Himalayas or desert.
- **Wind**: $P=\tfrac12\rho A v^3$, turbine gets $C_p P$ with $C_p\le0.593$ (Betz); doubling speed gives 8 times power.

All are renewable and clean in use; solar and wind are intermittent.

subtopics.title: Land degradation and desertification
subtopics.theory_md:
**Land degradation**: decline of the land's productive capacity through erosion, waterlogging, salinity, nutrient loss, pollution, mining and construction. About 30% of India's land is degraded.

**Human causes**: over-cultivation, **unrestricted grazing**, **deforestation**, poor irrigation (waterlogging, salinity).

**Desertification** (UNCCD): land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas from climatic variations and human activities. It is not the advance of existing deserts.

These activities strip plant cover so topsoil erodes: result **soil erosion and desertification**. Waterlogging results only from over-irrigation.
subtopics.basics_md: Plants hold soil in place. Take away the plants by cutting, over-grazing or over-ploughing, and wind and rain carry the soil away until only dry, barren land is left.
